title: Does English use the wrong word for clouds? | WEATHER WORDS

entries.note: Meteorology literally means the study of things high up in the air, though it no longer studies [[see:meteor]]s.
From Greek [[from:meteoron]], something high up; until the 15th century it meant any visible atmospheric phenomenon. Also covered in their space episode.
A Greek site with monasteries on huge rock formations; its name refers to places high up in the air, like [[same-root:meteor]].
What a [[see:meteor]] is called once it hits the ground.
What a [[see:meteor]] is called before it enters the Earth's atmosphere.
In early meteorology, tornadoes and other windstorms.
In early meteorology, water-based phenomena such as rain, snow, hail, dew, frost and clouds.
In early meteorology, light phenomena in the sky such as auroras and rainbows.
In early meteorology, fiery-looking things such as lightning and shooting stars.
From Old English [[from:weder]], with the D becoming TH around the 15th century; it once meant air, sky, storm or breeze, from a root meaning wind.
Probably went through the same D-to-TH change as [[see:weather]].
An Old English weather word, spelled with a G but soon pronounced much as today, reflecting the climate early speakers knew.
One of the weather words that has barely changed since Old English.
One of the weather words that has barely changed since Old English.
A barely changed Old English weather word that shares its root with [[same-root:weather]] and [[same-root:vent]].
One of the weather words that has barely changed since Old English.
One of the weather words that has barely changed since Old English.
In Old English it meant a rock, hill or heap; the hosts argue the word should really be [[see:wolcen]].
Shares the wind root of [[same-root:weather]].
A German word for weather; -witter is related to [[same-root:weather]], and the ge- prefix turns something into a noun.
Old English for bad weather, where un- means bad. This is odd because the root of [[see:weather]] means wind.
German for bad weather, the counterpart of Old English [[equivalent:unweder]].
A time-based Latin word for weather, linked to [[from:tempus]], time, and source of [[gave:tempest]].
A Greek word meaning seasonal time or weather.
Related to [[same-root:tempest]] through Latin [[from:tempus]], which meant both weather and time, ideas linked by seasonality.
Related to [[same-root:temperature]] through Latin [[from:tempus]], which meant both weather and time.
A misty rain, one of Britain's many words for rain.
A regional word for rain used in Shropshire.
One of Britain's many words for rain.
One of Britain's many regional words for rain.
One of Britain's many regional words for rain.
A Cumbrian word for rain.
One of Britain's many words for rain.
One of Britain's many words for rain.
One of Britain's many regional words for rain.
One of Britain's many regional words for rain.
A northern English word for rainy weather, quoted from 1894: "We've had nobbut softish weather all the week."
A Scottish dialect word for gross, icky rainy weather that sounds like what it means.
London Cockney rhyming slang for rain.
A rarely used word for rainy, related to the French word for rain; England is a very pluvious country.
A word related to [[same-root:pluvious]] with a similar meaning.
Literally falling head first, from Latin [[from:caput]], head. The rain sense dates from the late 17th century; early uses included casting evil angels from heaven.
Means to fall or happen suddenly, throw violently, or bring about; precipitating violence literally means going headlong into it. Related to [[same-root:precipitation]].
Means abrupt, sudden or steep; shares the head-first Latin root of [[same-root:precipitation]].
From Arabic [[from:mawsim]], season, passed through Portuguese [[from:monção]] and a Dutch form, which merged into the English word.
A mix of Greek [[from?:Typhon]], mythical father of storms, an Arabic word for a deluge found in the Quran, and possibly a Cantonese word for great wind.
Suggests something spinning; Jess grew up using it to mean a [[see:tornado]], but it also means a hurricane, especially around Oceania.
Coined in English in the early 1500s from Spanish [[from:tronada]], thunderstorm, reshuffled by metathesis under [[see:tornar]], to turn; Spanish later borrowed it back.
Earlier English forms like furacane came from Spanish and Portuguese, but today's word better reflects the Carib source [[from:huracan]].
Italian for oven, contrasted with Spanish [[same-root:horno]] to show Spanish F becoming H, as in [[see:hurricane]].
Spanish for oven, showing the F-to-H shift when compared with Italian [[same-root:forno]].
Once facienda, an example of Spanish F becoming H, from the Latin word for making and doing.
Loosely related to [[same-root:hacienda]] through the Latin word for making and doing.
The device that measures wind, from a Greek word for wind, [[from:anemos]].
Meaning life, spirit or breath; Jess first links it to [[see:anemometer]], and Rob says they share a root.
Etymologically a daughter of the wind; the sea anemone is named after the land plant.
Sea urchins are named after land urchins, or [[see:hedgehog]]s; street urchins are compared to little scurrying creatures.
The original land [[see:urchin]].
Simply a [[from:lightening]] of the sky, with the E dropped to tell the two words apart.
The source of [[gave:lightning]]; people still often write lightening for lightning.
Literally means loud noise and is loosely related to [[same-root:tone]]; its Old English form was [[see:Thunor]].
Loosely related to [[same-root:thunder]] far back.
Old English for thunder and the name of the Anglo-Saxon god equivalent to [[see:Thor]], the embodiment of thunder.
The Norse thunder god, equivalent to the Anglo-Saxon [[see:Thunor]].
Named after the god [[from:Thunor]], so it can equally be called thunder's day; discussed in an earlier episode.
From Dutch [[from:donderbus]], thunder gun.
Literally means something like to thunder down.
Santa's reindeer, originally Dunder and Blixem; the names combine Dutch [[from:donder]], thunder, and German Blitzen, lightning. Covered in their Christmas episode.
Means to explode or protest vehemently, from Latin [[from:fulmen]], lightning bolt.
Means to flash or sparkle, from a Latin word meaning glitter or vibrate; often misused by journalists, like [[see:excoriating]].
Another word that, like [[see:coruscate]], gets misused.
A Latin word for a downpour; nimbus in a cloud name marks it as a rain cloud. One of the cloud names Luke Howard coined.
The Old English word for cloud, related to German and Dutch [[same-root:Wolken]]; the hosts think it should be our word for cloud. It gave [[gave:welkin]].
German for clouds, a cognate of Old English [[same-root:wolcen]].
Dutch for clouds, spelled like the German but pronounced without the final N; a cognate of [[same-root:wolcen]].
A poetic word for the heavens, developed from [[from:wolcen]]; used by Shakespeare ("make the welkin ring") and into the 19th century.
A low, fluffy cloud whose name means heap; directly related to [[same-root:accumulation]]. Named by [[see:Luke Howard]] in 1802.
British amateur meteorologist who named [[see:cirrus]], [[see:cumulus]], [[see:stratus]] and [[see:nimbus]] clouds in 1802.
Means curl of hair in Latin; one of the cloud names coined by [[see:Luke Howard]].
A streaky, sheet-like spread of cloud; one of the names coined by [[see:Luke Howard]].
A hybrid cloud name meaning spread-out curls of hair.
A hybrid cloud name meaning a heap of curls.
A high-up spread of clouds.
A high-up heap of clouds.
A spread-out heap of clouds.
A heap of rain clouds: a huge, tall storm cloud, terrifying to fly over, with lightning flashing around it.
Directly related to [[same-root:cumulus]].
A thick, overall cloud cover that usually means rain and hides the sun.
White crystalline frost formed when water vapour freezes on cold surfaces; the rime in [[see:The Rime of the Ancient Mariner]], also a pun on [[see:rhyme]].

entries.term: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner
entries.note: Its title refers to the frost [[see:rime]], with a pun on [[see:rhyme]]; a poem about a frosty sea voyage and an albatross.
Once also spelled R-I-M-E, which makes the Ancient Mariner title a pun on [[see:rime]].
Means grey-haired frost, because it looks like grey hair collected on grass and branches; related to [[same-root:hoary]].
Describes someone with a big grey beard, like Gandalf; related to [[same-root:hoarfrost]].
Originally a ticket given when a baseball game was rained off, letting you come back another day; Rob had assumed it meant checking whether it would rain.
Spelled cheque in British English for the slip; every sense comes from chess, as their games episode explains, including the one in [[see:rain check]].
Means very cold, short for cold enough to freeze the balls off a brass monkey (popular brass souvenirs); the cannonball-rack theory has no evidence behind it.
An American expression for very cold; "as balls" is a general intensifier among millennials, related in sense to [[see:brass monkeys]].
English term for very dense fog, especially industrial [[see:smog]] before the Clean Air Act, which was as thick as pea soup.
Smoky fog, the kind meant by [[see:pea souper]].
The smell of rain, literally rock plus ichor, the fluid in the gods' veins; Jess says it means "rock snot" and is only loved for its meaning.
A bacterial compound released from dry soil by rain that causes [[see:petrichor]]; Jess prefers it as a word.
Wind-blown spray from cresting wave tops during high winds and gales; also the name of one of Jess's favourite wines.
